context.transcript_excerpt: Welcome to the Prosperity Podcast with me, Nicole Bremner, an investor and entrepreneur. Along with discussions around investing, I'm currently serializing my book, Bricked It, the story of building and losing a multi-million pound property portfolio. Let's get into it. Chapter 8. A man is not a financial plan. Now that you have the safer system, you can put it into practice whenever a suitable investment opportunity comes your way. With practice, you'll be able to run through the system and quickly exclude any opportunities that are potentially destabilizing. By doing this every single time, you'll feel that sense of empowerment knowing that you have a system in place to keep you and your money safe. It helps cut through the noise and uncertainty and also deepens your trust in yourself. With that said, there is something that we need to address. I was talking to Anya, another client, when her eyes welled up. I love my husband. He's a good father to our children and a good person. But what happens if things change? He has an affair or worse, dies. What will happen to us then? Anya is right to be concerned. Her husband oversees their finances and makes all the final decisions. He works in banking, though Anya can't quite explain what he does specifically. Don't misread the situation. Anya is no hapless housewife. She's an intelligent woman running a successful PR firm she founded with her best friend from uni. She can write the most engaging press release, but numbers just aren't her thing. Anya has no idea how much they have saved, where it's invested, or even what her husband earns. All she knows is that household expenses are covered and she draws a salary from her company for any extras. Another example is a school friend's mother, Dorothy. Her life revolved around her only son and she never worked outside the home. Once he left Australia to travel the world, she found herself approaching 70 with no career or money. She was stuck at home with a grumpy old man she had nothing in common with and, quite frankly, didn't even like. Dorothy had never even had a debit card in her life, let alone know how to use one. Determined to completely change her life, Dorothy divorced her husband. she and another single female friend bought round the world tickets to Europe and a backpack to set off on the adventure of their lifetimes staying in hostels and traveling the European train network at 70. We owe it to ourselves to take back some control over our own financial situation we constantly having things dumbed down for us like girl maths it no wonder we leave the financial decisions to the men in our lives If you reading this book you must have a strong desire to become more financially literate I urge you to consider yourself as a separate financial entity to your partner No matter how many years you've been together or how happy you are, if the worst happens and you're left bereft and without quick access to funds, it will be so much worse. Sit down right now and get a grasp on your own finances. As we discussed back in chapter four, you should have three months of cash easily accessible at all times, not in a joint account, in your own account. Make sure you're in a strong financial position and are empowered to make your own decisions that impact your life. Anya from earlier in this chapter said, I wish I had saved more money rather than spend it on expensive handbags that now sit in my wardrobe. sadly as women we have what I call a female tax we're bombarded with images of how we should look and how we should dress which is expensive to maintain hair color and cut 200 pounds botox 250 pounds hair removal 75 pounds nails 40 pounds latest beauty products and makeup 50 pounds must have handbag 1200 pounds shoes clothes stop yes it's amazing to look and feel fabulous but to what end and at what cost i'm not telling you to look like a hairy mousy woman wearing holy sweats i'm urging you to be mindful of this tax that is imposed upon us

pending_qa.q: How should individuals calculate their net worth and what assets should be included?
pending_qa.r: Begin by listing all investments, cash, ISAs, your home, car, gold, Bitcoin and everything of value in one column, then list related debts like mortgages or car finance in the next column, and unsecured debt like credit cards and personal loans in a third column. Subtract debt from assets to calculate net worth realistically, valuing items at what they would sell for within a couple of months.

pending_qa.q: What are the average UK savings benchmarks by age group according to recent data?
pending_qa.r: According to 2022 Office of National Statistics data, average UK savings for ages 25 to 34 are between £500 and £5,000; ages 35 to 44 between £5,000 and £12,500; ages 45 to 54 between £5,000 and £12,500; ages 55 to 64 between £12,000 and £25,000; and ages 65 plus between £25,000 and £50,000. To reach the top 25% of your age group, ages 25 to 34 need over £12,500, ages 35 to 44 over £25,000, ages 45 to 54 over £50,000, and ages 55 plus over £100,000.

pending_qa.q: What percentage of young adults in the UK have no savings or carry significant debt?
pending_qa.r: At least 25% of those under 54 either have no savings or are in debt. Additionally, 38% of 25 to 34 year olds are in debt with 23% of that age group carrying over £5,000 in debt, most likely from student loans.

pending_qa.q: How can subscription services and recurring expenses significantly impact annual savings?
pending_qa.r: While skipping individual lattes makes minimal difference, a £36 monthly subscription such as Apple Plus costs £432 per year, and when combined with other recurring subscriptions that accumulate unnoticed, the annual impact becomes substantial. Being ruthless about eliminating unnecessary recurring expenditures without compromising your overall lifestyle can free up significant funds for savings.
